hook: A furniture workshop owner in a city full of carpenters cannot set the pay; if she offers less than the going wage, nobody shows up. What she can decide is how many carpenters to hire. Each one adds chairs worth a certain amount and costs the going wage. Her whole decision is a comparison of those two numbers.

A competitive firm produces the quantity where
prereq.why: Produce while the next unit adds at least as much to revenue as to cost.

prereq.q: A rise in market labor demand moves the wage
options: in a direction that is indeterminate
prereq.why: Labor demand shifts right along labor supply.

figure.caption: The market sets the wage WM. The firm takes it as a horizontal line, S = MFC = W, and hires qF workers, where its MRP meets that line.

chain.cause: Market labor demand and supply set the wage
chain.effect: each small firm takes that wage as given

chain.cause: The firm can hire any number of workers at that wage
chain.effect: its MRC (MFC) is the wage: a horizontal line

chain.cause: Each worker adds MRP to revenue and the wage to cost
chain.effect: the firm hires up to where MRP = MRC

chain.cause: A fixed cost changes neither MRP nor MRC
chain.effect: the number hired stays the same

ideas: A firm in a perfectly competitive labor market is a wage taker. Draw the market and the firm side by side; carry the wage across as the line S = MFC = W.
Marginal resource cost (MRC, also MFC) = change in total labor cost ÷ change in workers. For a wage taker, MRC = W.
Hiring rule: hire where MRP = MRC; from a table, the last worker whose MRP is at least the MRC. Fixed costs do not change it.
Least-cost rule: MP of labor ÷ wage = MP of capital ÷ rental price. Spend more on the input with the higher MP per dollar.

misconception.wrong: When its rent rises, a firm should hire fewer workers to keep costs down.
misconception.right: Rent is a fixed cost: it is paid whatever the number of workers. Each worker still adds the same MRP and costs the same wage, so the profit-maximizing number of workers does not change.

summary: In a perfectly competitive labor market the wage is set where market labor demand meets labor supply, and each firm is a wage taker facing a horizontal line S = MFC = W. A firm maximizes profit by hiring where MRP = MRC, which from a table is the last worker whose MRP is at least the wage. A higher wage means fewer workers, a higher product price or productivity means more, and a fixed cost changes nothing. To make any output at the least cost, the MP per dollar must be equal across inputs.
